E1.title: Species distribution
E1.text: social factors include land use and water availability.

E2.title: Species distribution
E2.text: An example of the effects of abiotic factors on species distribution can be seen in drier areas, where most individuals of a species will gather around water sources, forming a clumped distribution.

E5.title: Species distribution
E5.text: Range is often described with the following qualities:

E6.title: Species distribution
E6.text: One key factor in determining species distribution is the phenology of the organism.

E7.title: Species distribution
E7.text: Plants are well documented as examples showing how phenology is an adaptive trait that can influence fitness in changing climates.

E8.title: Species distribution
E8.text: Physiology can influence species distributions in an environmentally sensitive manner because physiology underlies movement such as exploration and dispersal.

E9.title: Species distribution
E9.text: Individuals that are more disperse-prone have higher metabolism, locomotor performance, corticosterone levels, and immunity.

E11.title: Species distribution
E11.text: Distribution patterns may change by season, distribution by humans, in response to the availability of resources, and other abiotic and biotic factors.

E12.title: Species distribution
E12.text: climatic factors consist of sunlight, atmosphere, humidity, temperature, and salinity;

E14.title: Species distribution
E14.text: Biotic factors such as predation, disease, and inter- and intra-specific competition for resources such as food, water, and mates can also affect how a species is distributed.

E15.title: Species distribution
E15.text: For example, biotic factors in a quail's environment would include their prey (insects and seeds), competition from other quail, and their predators, such as the coyote.

E16.title: Species distribution
E16.text: An advantage of a herd, community, or other clumped distribution allows a population to detect predators earlier, at a greater distance, and potentially mount an effective defense.

E17.title: Species distribution
E17.text: Due to limited resources, populations may be evenly distributed to minimize competition, as is found in forests, where competition for sunlight produces an even distribution of trees.

E19.title: Species distribution
E19.text: This simple SDM is often modified through the use of range data or ancillary information, such as elevation or water distance.

E20.title: Species distribution
E20.text: One common example of bird species' ranges are land mass areas bordering water bodies, such as oceans, rivers, or lakes; they are called a coastal strip.

E21.title: Species distribution
E21.text: A second example, some species of bird depend on water, usually a river, swamp, etc., or water related forest and live in a river corridor.

E22.title: Species distribution
E22.text: A separate example of a river corridor would be a river corridor that includes the entire drainage, having the edge of the range delimited by mountains, or higher elevations; the river itself would be a smaller percentage of this entire wildlife corridor, but the corridor is created because of the river.

E23.title: Species distribution
E23.text: In biology, the range of a species is the geographical area within which that species can be found.

E24.title: Species distribution
E24.text: Within that range, distribution is the general structure of the species population, while dispersion is the variation in its population density.

E25.title: Species distribution
E25.text: The Species Distribution Grids Project is an effort led out of the University of Columbia to create maps and databases of the whereabouts of various animal species.

E26.title: Species distribution
E26.text: This work is centered on preventing deforestation and prioritizing areas based on species richness.

E27.title: Species distribution
E27.text: As of April 2009, data are available for global amphibian distributions, as well as birds and mammals in the Americas.

E28.title: Species distribution
E28.text: The map gallery Gridded Species Distribution contains sample maps for the Species Grids data set.

E29.title: Species distribution
E29.text: These maps are not inclusive but rather contain a representative sample of the types of data available for download:

E30.title: Species distribution
E30.text: Species distribution can be predicted based on the pattern of biodiversity at spatial scales.

E31.title: Species distribution
E31.text: A general hierarchical model can integrate disturbance, dispersal and population dynamics.

E32.title: Species distribution
E32.text: Based on factors of dispersal, disturbance, resources limiting climate, and other species distribution, predictions of species distribution can create a bio-climate range, or bio-climate envelope.

E33.title: Species distribution
E33.text: The envelope can range from a local to a global scale or from a density independence to dependence.

E34.title: Species distribution
E34.text: The hierarchical model takes into consideration the requirements, impacts or resources as well as local extinctions in disturbance factors.

E35.title: Species distribution
E35.text: Models can integrate the dispersal/migration model, the disturbance model, and abundance model.

E36.title: Species distribution
E36.text: Species distribution models (SDMs) can be used to assess climate change impacts and conservation management issues.

E37.title: Species distribution
E37.text: Species distribution models include: presence/absence models, the dispersal/migration models, disturbance models, and abundance models.

E38.title: Species distribution
E38.text: A prevalent way of creating predicted distribution maps for different species is to reclassify a land cover layer depending on whether or not the species in question would be predicted to habit each cover

E39.title: Species distribution
E39.text: For mobile animals, the term natural range is often used, as opposed to areas where it occurs as a vagrant.

E40.title: Species distribution
E40.text: On large scales, the pattern of distribution among individuals in a population is clumped.
